prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Booking Holdings Inc." (ticker BKNG). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Booking is the top dog in online travel with a strong brand and network, but it is a mature leader in an established industry, the stock has fallen about 19% over the past year rather than showing momentum, and it is seen as cheap rather than overvalued. It fits Gardner's quality traits better than his emerging-industry and momentum traits.
summaries.buffett: Booking is an understandable, highly profitable marketplace with a 32.8% operating margin in 2025, about $9.1B of free cash flow and a long record of shrinking its share count. Debt slightly exceeds cash and equity is negative due to buybacks, but at roughly 15-16 times forward earnings it looks like a wonderful business at a fair price.
summaries.munger: The two-sided network of about 4.4 million properties and 1.2 billion yearly room nights is a durable, simple moat run by rational capital allocators. Inverting, the main ways it fails are AI assistants or Google capturing the traveller relationship and regulators curbing its fees, which are real but slow-moving risks.
summaries.lynch: Booking is a stalwart: steady high-single to low-double digit revenue growth, mid-teens EPS growth from buybacks, and a forward P/E of about 15-16 that gives a PEG near 1. The story is simple, but it is a well-followed large cap rather than an overlooked bargain.
summaries.fisher: Booking keeps adding products (flights, attractions, payments, AI trip planning) under its Connected Trip strategy and is exceptionally good at performance marketing. Its management is long-tenured and shareholder-minded, though product innovation is incremental rather than research-driven.
summaries.graham: Booking passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and earnings-growth tests, but fails on dividend history (paid only since 2024), price relative to three-year average earnings (about 24 times) and book value, which is negative. It does not qualify as a defensive Graham stock.
summaries.thiel: Booking has a quasi-monopoly position in Europe's online hotel booking and strong distribution, but its technology is not ten times better than rivals' and it did not start from a small niche it dominates. Its biggest Thiel-style risk is that AI agents become the new monopoly gatekeeper in travel.
summaries.gerstner: Booking shows the profitable, disciplined growth Gerstner prizes, with a 36% adjusted EBITDA margin, a cost-transformation program and large buybacks. Whether it benefits from or is disrupted by AI agents is the key debate, and the stock's 2026 de-rating suggests the market leans worried.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are still growing at mid-teens rates and estimates have edged up, but the stock has trended down for a year and guidance points to slower growth amid Middle East-related travel softness. It lacks the accelerating-earnings and price-momentum setup Druckenmiller looks for.
summaries.smith: Booking has high returns on capital, about 34% free-cash-flow margins, low capital needs and resilient demand, the hallmarks of a Fundsmith-style good company. At a free-cash-flow yield near 7.8% the price is not demanding, though its reliance on Google traffic is a long-term concern.
summaries.greenblatt: With trailing operating income of about $9.3B against an enterprise value of about $126B (an earnings yield near 7.4%) and extremely high return on capital, Booking scores well on the Magic Formula's two measures.
summaries.akre: Booking fits Akre's three-legged stool well: an outstanding business with high returns, skilled and shareholder-focused management, and free cash flow reinvested mostly into buybacks. The weaker leg is reinvestment opportunity, since much of the cash is returned rather than redeployed at high returns.
summaries.pabrai: Booking is a simple, durable business trading at a modest multiple after a fall in its share price, offering limited downside from its free-cash-flow generation. It is not, however, a distressed situation with heads-I-win odds; the setback is mild and the AI risk is real.
summaries.wood: Booking is not an innovation-platform company in ARK's sense; it is an incumbent that could either harness AI agents or be disrupted by them. It does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation framework.
summaries.ackman: Booking matches many of Pershing Square's criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with high barriers to entry, limited exposure to commodities and a fair valuation. Its balance sheet carries more debt than cash and negative equity, and travel remains sensitive to macro shocks.
summaries.sleep: Booking's scale lets it outspend rivals on marketing and offer the widest choice, a scale-economies-shared dynamic, but it largely keeps the benefits as margin rather than passing them to customers through lower prices. It is a strong business but not a classic Nomad-style scale-economies-shared story.
summaries.valentine: Booking solves a large problem (finding and booking travel worldwide) and has a huge market, but it is a mature incumbent rather than the early-stage, timing-driven opportunity Valentine sought.
summaries.nash: Booking scores well on quality (32.9% trailing operating margin, revenue growth plus FCF margin near 47, revenue growing faster than expenses) and on value, with a Nash DCF near $210 per share versus $163 at 12%. It fails Nash's instant-kill test because debt ($20.2B) exceeds cash ($17.2B), it does not ride an AI-style secular trend, and it is exposed to EU regulation.

momentum.evidence: The share price fell from about $201 (split-adjusted) in October 2025 to $163.45 on October 16, 2026, roughly -19% over a year, lagging the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Glenn Fogel has led strongly since 2017 and the stock is widely held by institutions (37 analysts, 30 Buy-rated), but no single famous investor or partner stands out as a backer.

g6.evidence: Commentators mostly call it cheap, with a consensus price target around $234 versus a $163 share price.

simple.evidence: It takes a commission on hotel stays and other travel booked through Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda and KAYAK, a model any generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Apart from the 2020 pandemic year, Booking has grown bookings and profits for two decades; revenue rose every year from $6.8B (2020) to $26.9B (2025).

integrity.evidence: Management is candid and rational with capital (shares down from 1,029M in 2020 to 770M diluted in Q2 2026), but it has faced repeated antitrust findings in Europe, such as Spain's €413.2M CNMC fine.

b6.evidence: Since the large KAYAK and OpenTable deals of the early 2010s it has avoided big acquisitions and returned cash through buybacks and dividends.

roic.evidence: Operating income of $8.8B in 2025 against a small asset base (debt is largely offset by $17.2B of cash and the business needs little capital) gives very high returns on invested capital.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $9.1B ($9,409M operating cash flow minus $322M capex), well above net income of $5.4B.

b10.evidence: Most retained cash has gone into buybacks ($6.4B in 2025, $7.8B in H1 2026), which cut the share count but have been made at prices above today's, leaving retained-earnings value creation positive but recently modest.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF (12% discount rate) gives roughly $210 per share versus $163.45, a margin of about 22%, but AI and regulatory risk make that estimate uncertain.

fairprice.evidence: About 15.6 times FY2026 consensus EPS of $10.45 and a 7.8% free-cash-flow yield is reasonable for a business with 33% operating margins and mid-teens EPS growth.

mu5.evidence: The main failure paths are AI agents or Google owning the traveller, regulators capping commissions, and travel shocks, a short but serious list.

reinvest.evidence: Booking needs little capital (capex $322M in 2025) so most profit is returned rather than reinvested; new areas like flights and attractions offer limited reinvestment scale.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart: steady high-single-digit revenue growth, mid-teens EPS growth from buybacks, and a simple story of more travel booked online.

ly3.evidence: Forward P/E of about 15.6 against consensus FY2026 adjusted EPS growth of about 14.6% gives a ratio close to, but slightly above, 1.

runway.evidence: Room nights still grow (+5% in Q2 2026) and flights, attractions and alternative homes add runway, but core hotel booking is maturing.

ly7.evidence: The company is cutting its share count fast (44 million shares repurchased in H1 2026), but insiders are not open-market buyers.

ly8.evidence: It is a $120B+ large cap covered by about 37 analysts.

fi2.evidence: Management is building the Connected Trip (flights, attractions, payments) and Gen AI tools such as its AI trip planner and partner Smart Messenger.

fi3.evidence: Technology spending produced fast growth in flights (+37% tickets in 2025) and attractions, but no breakthrough product beyond its core marketplace.

fi4.evidence: It is the most skilled performance marketer in travel, spending $8.2B on marketing in 2025 while still earning a 32.8% operating margin.

longterm.evidence: It invests in long-term areas like the Connected Trip and AI while also running a cost transformation program and heavy buybacks focused on near-term EPS.

gr1.evidence: Revenue of $26.9B in 2025 and a market value around $123B.

ni10.evidence: Net income stayed positive even in the 2020 pandemic year ($59M) and was $5.4B in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Booking only began paying a dividend in 2024 (none was paid in 2023).

eps10.evidence: Pre-split diluted EPS rose to $165.57 in 2025 from $76.35 in 2022, far more than one third above the level of a decade earlier.

gr6.evidence: Market value of about $123B is roughly 24 times average 2023-2025 net income of $5.2B.

gr7.evidence: Book value is negative (stockholders' deficit of -$10.8B at June 2026), so P/E × P/B cannot meet Graham's test.

th1.evidence: Its technology is good but not ten times better than Expedia's, Airbnb's or Google's.

timing.evidence: Travel demand remains resilient, but AI-agent disruption and 2026 Middle East-related softness make timing less favourable.

th3.evidence: Booking.com started by dominating European online hotel booking and expanded globally, though it now operates in a large mature market.

team.evidence: Glenn Fogel is a seasoned, capable CEO (with the company since 2000), but not a celebrated founder.

th5.evidence: Its distribution engine, $8.2B of yearly marketing plus a growing direct and app channel, is its key strength.

durable.evidence: Its supply network is durable, but AI assistants and Google could change how travellers start trips within 10 to 20 years.

th7.evidence: Online travel is a well-understood, competitive market with no hidden opportunity.

trend.evidence: It benefits from the long shift of travel online and could use AI to sell more, but AI may also benefit rivals like Google and OpenAI more.

dr1.evidence: Q2 2026 adjusted EPS rose 15% and FY2026 estimates edged up after results, but revenue growth guidance slowed to 4-6% for Q3 2026.

dr2.evidence: About $650M of transformation savings by end-2027 and buybacks should lift EPS, but that is largely expected.

dr4.evidence: Healthy consumer travel demand helps, but geopolitical shocks and a higher interest bill on $20.2B of debt work against it.

dr6.evidence: Possible catalysts include a rebound in Middle East-affected travel, cost savings and AI-agent partnerships.

dr7.evidence: Business quality supports a meaningful position, but AI disruption risk argues against a highly concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Booking reports no gross margin; its direct sales and other expenses were only 12.8% of 2025 revenue, implying high gross profitability, though marketing costs are large.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $9.5B against a $123B market value is a 7.8% yield.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $9.3B against an enterprise value of about $126B is a 7.4% earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The 2026 slowdown tied to the Middle East conflict and AI fears looks temporary, but AI disruption is a structural question.

pa4.evidence: Strong free cash flow, $17.2B of cash and a dominant marketplace make permanent loss unlikely at this valuation.

wo1.evidence: Booking uses AI but is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: Its costs do not fall sharply with volume in a way that opens large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It is a single online-travel platform, not a combination of innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Travel is already a huge market growing in single digits; it will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: It holds no commodities, but travel demand depends on the economy, fuel-driven flight prices and geopolitics.

ns1.evidence: Scale funds Genius discounts and better choice, but Booking keeps much of its scale advantage as margin.

ns4.evidence: Its position depends on how AI agents reshape travel distribution, which is uncertain.

va2.evidence: It solves the painful job of finding, comparing and safely booking accommodation anywhere in the world.

tn1.evidence: Online travel is an established market rather than a secular trend like AI or energy infrastructure.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as an online travel agency and that is what it is becoming, with no hidden transformation.

tn3.evidence: It is a US large cap, but travel is seasonal and cyclical.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year since 2020 and it is highly profitable, passing two of three; debt ($20.2B) exceeds cash ($17.2B) because of buyback borrowing.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive every quarter, but debt has exceeded cash (e.g. $20.2B vs $17.2B at June 2026; $18.7B vs $17.2B at December 2025).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 13.4% in 2025, but 2026 guidance is high single digits.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 13.4% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 33.8% is about 47.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 13.4% while total operating expenses grew 11.8%.

tn9.evidence: It fails the more-debt-than-cash test ($20.2B debt vs $17.2B cash at June 2026), though it passes on size, operating margin (32.9%) and age.

tn10.evidence: It faces the EU Digital Markets Act gatekeeper regime, Spain's €413.2M CNMC fine (under appeal) and a Dutch consumer class claim.

tn11.evidence: It provides an online marketplace that helps travellers find and book stays and trips and helps hotels fill rooms, and charges hotels a commission on each booking, chosen for its unmatched selection.

tn13.evidence: Total about 80: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue vs expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue and free cash flow rose every year 2021-2025, but operating margin dipped in 2023 (27.3% from 29.9%) and debt exceeded cash at end-2025.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is 5.5x (2025) and the current ratio 1.09, but assets excluding goodwill ($27.0B) are below liabilities ($40.5B) and equity is negative.

tn18.evidence: Fogel has a strong execution record and nearly 10 years as CEO, but he is not a founder and has not made open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Booking beat adjusted EPS estimates in Q1 2026 ($1.14 vs $1.07 expected) and Q2 2026, continuing a long record of beats.

tn21.evidence: No fraud, co-CEOs or acquisition spree, but there are recurring antitrust findings and a 2025 $457M impairment.

tn22.evidence: It has $26.9B of revenue, strong profits and shrinks its share count rather than issuing stock.

tn24.evidence: At a 7.8% free-cash-flow yield the price implies only low-single-digit growth, below the 8-13% revenue growth Booking is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using about 12% growth and a 33% FCF margin over five years, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate, value is about $210 per share versus $163.45.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 15.6 is modest versus quality peers, but PEG is about 1.07 (15.6 ÷ 14.6% EPS growth), just above 1.
